funding: Run by the City of Mannheim. Its 2018 building (€68.3M) was funded by Hector Stiftung II (€50M, from SAP co-founder Hans-Werner Hector), the city (€10M), Baden-Württemberg (€2.62M) and about €4.9M in private gifts; a Stifterkreis of 57 unnamed members and the Förderkreis also give support.
why_flagged: In 2018 the museum found Nazi-looted art in its collection and listed 25 further suspect works.
other_findings: In 2018 the museum identified Wilhelm Leibl's The Drinker (1874), acquired from a Nazi agency, as looted, and listed 25 other works suspected of being looted or sold under duress (Wikipedia).
bottom_line: A city-run museum whose 2018 building was mostly paid for by SAP co-founder Hans-Werner Hector's foundation, with smaller city and state shares. No flagged funder was found. Worth watching: the provenance research on works acquired 1933–45, and the unnamed Stifterkreis members.
changes: Adds the full building budget: €68.3M, of which €50M came from Hector Stiftung II Kunst gGmbH, €10M from the city, €2.62M from the state and about €4.9M from private gifts.
Identifies Hans-Werner Hector as an SAP co-founder.
Adds Kunsthallen Ausstellungs GmbH as an exhibition endowment.
Adds the Nazi-era provenance finding (2018) as a flag.
Names the Stifterkreis Stiftungsrat chair (Dr Susanne Fuchs) and its city members; members themselves are still unnamed.

funding: Funded mainly by private foundations and individuals: 2024 revenue $6.4M, with government grants under 5%. funders: Lenore S. & Bernard A. Greenberg Fund
bottom_line: Funded by Texas family foundations (Brown, Sarofim), arts foundations and individual collectors, with very little public money. No flagged funder was found. Worth watching: large gifts through donor-advised funds and anonymous donors at the $1M level, which hide where the money comes from.

not_related: Chinati Foundation — also founded by Donald Judd in Marfa, but a separate non-profit (EIN 74-2340423).

funding: Funded by Fondation Alliances, the charitable foundation of the Lazraq family's listed property developer Groupe Alliances; it gave significant support for the 2023–25 overhaul. No other funder is named.
flags: Sole corporate funder with debt crisis
why_flagged: The museum depends entirely on Groupe Alliances, which was suspended from the Casablanca exchange in 2016 with about 8.5 billion dirhams of debt.
other_findings: Groupe Alliances was suspended from the Casablanca Stock Exchange in 2016 with debt of nearly 8.5 billion dirhams. Asset transfers cut it to 2 billion dirhams by end-2018, and the company reported a return to profit from 2019 (Challenge.ma).
A Telquel headline (29 Dec 2015) says Alami Lazraq lost Alliances' construction subsidiaries.
bottom_line: The museum is a single-family corporate foundation project with no other named funder or published accounts. No misconduct at the museum was found. Worth watching: its full dependence on Groupe Alliances, whose 2015–2018 debt crisis shows how exposed the museum is to the company's fortunes.
changes: Adds Alami Lazraq as co-founder and collector (The Art Newspaper).
Adds the 2023 earthquake closure and the 2 Feb 2025 reopening.
Adds Groupe Alliances' 2016 suspension and debt restructuring as a flag.
Records The Art Newspaper's description of Alliances as Morocco's largest hotel builder.

funding: Core operating funding from Creative Australia and Creative Victoria, with City of Melbourne and Victorian Department of Education programme funding. Private support comes from the Ian Potter and Robert Salzer foundations, individual donors (several of them board members) and corporate partners including Dulux, KWM and Wood Marsh.
funders: J. Andrew Cook & Prof. Wendy Brown
bottom_line: A free, publicly core-funded art centre topped up by a group of private donors, several of whom are board members. No flagged funder or protest was found. Worth watching: the overlap between major donors and the board.
